chapter: South America and back in New York
title: Musicians' restaurants and why a band is everyone's work
summary: Over breakfast at Johnny Johnson's and Glenn's, bands made plans, and he argues every member contributes, comparing it to Notre Dame and baseball teams.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: What about places that didn't feature music. Where performers would hang out. What places were there?

Well, there was two restaurants. There was a restaurant called Johnny Johnson's and there was the Blue Grass, and then there was Glenn's. Now, these restaurants, we used to go there when we come up from the Club Alabam. And, after

we came back. Where musicians set there and built plans and dreamed. Of course, your breakfast would always consist of an order of hotcakes, two pork chops and three scrambled eggs and coffee and things like that. Of course, some of the boys would drink, but I didn't bother with much of that. But that was the breakfast. That's what was served. Hotcakes and maybe three scrambled eggs and some sausage and potatoes and -- french fried potatoes or home fried potatoes. Well, you see, but when we sit there, that's where you make the brotherhood in a band, and amongst your friends. We set there and we think up ideas, man and a guy say, "Look Sam." Because nobody makes a band alone. A band consists of just as many members as you have in that band. And so, but he has his -- the leader must know what to take and what not to take. But the whole band, no-one can say that he made a band. That is out there from Jim Europe or Duke Ellington right on down the line, you cannot say this man has done it all by himself. Everybody contributes to a band. And everybody's absolutely necessary in a band. It's like a lot of people say. Well, take a football team. Knute Rockne, Rockne and Notre Dame. Yeah, the quarterback is good. But how's he going to get the ball to be good with it if the center, if the two guards are not strong to hold the line until he can throw the ball. And he can throw a pass, but if you don't have an end to catch that pass, and the man's fast enough to run. You don't have Jim Brown or this last boy, O.J. Simpson, to hit the line

and go through. Well, you used to be getting the ball. So, I mean, but everybody -- which is very wrong, even with a baseball team. They'll holler, Tom Seaver. Well, Tom Seaver gets hit, but if there wasn't somebody out there to catch that ball and throw it, when you have a no-hit game, for instance. You have struck out everybody, but the man -- your supporting cast. I think it's very wrong that the newspapers come out and say, 'Tom Seaver did this.' Or it's very wrong to do that.
